title: Nutrition is becoming a converging climate, health, and financing problem as healthy diets remain unaffordable and delivery systems stay fragmented
source_unit: 2026 Global Nutrition Report: Integrating food and health systems for climate-resilient nutrition, Global Nutrition Report
geography: Global nutrition, food-system, health-system, climate, financing, and equity evidence, with particular attention to low- and middle-income countries

observations.period: 2026 report; global healthy-diet affordability and nutrition progress

denominator.unit: global nutrition and healthy-diet evidence frame

healthy_diet_affordability.unit: billion people unable to afford a healthy diet

target_progress.value: progress towards global nutrition targets and SDGs 2 and 3 remains off track

malnutrition_pattern.value: undernutrition persists while overweight, obesity, and diet-related non-communicable diseases rise

observations.method: Synthesis of global nutrition, diet-affordability, food-system, health-system, and commitment-accountability evidence presented in the report.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate and progress assessment are reported at global scale; they do not by themselves identify local causal pathways, household-level change, or the effect of a particular intervention.
observations.subgroup: People unable to afford healthy diets, with burdens concentrated in low- and middle-income countries and overlapping risks across life stages.
observations.counterinterpretation: Global off-track progress can coexist with improvement in particular countries, population groups, or nutrition outcomes; the report is a global synthesis rather than a uniform country ranking.

observations.period: 2026 report; climate shocks and nutrition pathways

climate_effects.value: long-term climate shifts and more frequent extreme weather can lower agricultural productivity, reduce the nutritional value of some staple crops, and raise food prices

health_infrastructure.value: climate pressures can damage health and sanitation infrastructure and increase climate-sensitive disease burdens

compound_shocks.value: climate effects interact with conflict, pandemics, and economic crises to disrupt food value chains and health services

observations.method: Review and integration of evidence on climate, food systems, health systems, conflict, pandemic, and economic-crisis interactions.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies linked mechanisms and system pressures; the magnitude and timing of effects vary by location, crop, infrastructure, income, governance, and response capacity.
observations.subgroup: Food producers, households facing food-price shocks, people dependent on disrupted health or sanitation services, and communities exposed to climate-sensitive disease.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate-resilient production, social protection, service adaptation, and targeted nutrition action can reduce exposure and protect diets; disruption is not an inevitable outcome of every shock.

denominator.unit: report framework for achieving healthy diets under climate change

system_integration.value: healthy diets depend on food systems, health systems, and social protection working together rather than advancing in parallel

enabling_functions.value: leadership and governance, financing, operational capacity, and research, monitoring, and data

delivery_route.value: nutrition can be anchored in universal health coverage and primary healthcare while linking to social protection and climate policy

observations.method: Analytical framework synthesis connecting food, health, social protection, climate, finance, governance, delivery, and data functions.
observations.uncertainty: The framework is a practical organizing model, not a causal impact estimate; implementation feasibility depends on national institutions, fiscal space, coordination, and local priorities.
observations.subgroup: Governments, donors, development banks, climate-finance providers, health and food-system implementers, civil society, women’s organisations, and frontline providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Integration can create coordination costs or obscure sector-specific accountability if roles, indicators, financing, and trade-offs are not explicit.

observations.period: 2026 report; nutrition commitments and financing accountability

denominator.unit: N4G Tokyo 2021 and Paris 2025 commitment analysis

smart_commitments.value: more than half of government commitments at the N4G Paris Summit achieved high or upper-moderate SMART scores

food_system_indicators.unit: percent of analysed commitments using monitoring indicators aligned with specific food-systems frameworks

resilience_integration.value: resilience considerations appeared in nearly three-quarters of commitments explicitly linking food and health systems, while they were largely absent from single-system commitments

observations.method: Comparative analysis of nutrition commitments for procedural SMART quality, financing, monitoring indicators, resilience, and cross-system alignment.
observations.uncertainty: Commitment quality and stated alignment do not establish implementation, spending, service delivery, or nutrition impact; the denominators and coding rules are defined in the report’s commitment analysis.
observations.subgroup: Governments and commitment-makers, donors, accountability bodies, implementing institutions, and populations relying on nutrition and health services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Procedural commitments can still be useful as a coordination and accountability base, and missing indicators or financing in a commitment does not prove that no related action or funding exists elsewhere.

related_sources.claim: Full official 2026 Global Nutrition Report PDF.
Official foreword describing the integrated food-health framework and four enabling functions.
Official conclusion with priority routes for governments, donors, development banks, and climate-finance providers.

boundary: This record adds a global nutrition, climate-resilience, food-health systems, social protection, financing, gender-equity, and accountability route. It uses public report-level evidence, not respondent-level ingestion, household microdata, a causal estimate of climate effects, a forecast of future nutrition outcomes, or proof that integrated policy will succeed in every setting.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Global Nutrition Report landing page, executive summary, introduction, foreword, conclusion, and full-report link reviewed for healthy-diet affordability, off-track nutrition progress, climate-food-health pathways, system integration, framework functions, and commitment-accountability findings.
